opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
I wrestle with this passage in the Gospel of John.  The tension in this passage is intentional. At first glance, it almost sounds impossible, even uncomfortable. Greater than Christ? How could that even be said?  Firstly, the important thing is this: Jesus was not speaking casually when He said it. In the Gospel of John 14:12, Christ says:
“Whoever believes in me will do the works that I do, and will do greater ones than these, because I am going to the Father.”
But notice something important: Jesus ties the statement directly to “because I am going to the Father.” He is not saying human beings suddenly become greater than God. He is saying that once He returns to the Father, the Holy Spirit will be poured out through Him into the Church. The work of Christ will no longer remain confined to one geographic place, one body walking physically through Galilee. It will spread outward through believers across nations and centuries.
In that sense, the “greater works” become greater in reach. Greater in extent. The Gospel is moving across the world. Souls brought into eternal life through Christ. The Church continues His work through the power of the Holy Spirit.
Jesus is continually trying to move the disciples beyond seeing Him merely as a man standing in front of them. He is revealing union with the Father.  “If you see me, you see the Father.”
This is why belief matters so deeply—not belief as intellectual agreement, but participation. Allowing Christ to dwell within you. We hear the phrase, if you only had faith, even faith the size of a mustard seed.  Well, that seems easy, but apparently, I cannot move mountains.  But it is not about our humanity being a disqualification, because Scripture repeatedly shows the opposite. The apostles themselves doubted constantly:
Peter sank into the water.
Thomas doubted the resurrection.
The disciples fled.
Paul called himself the chief of sinners.
The presence of struggle does not prove the absence of faith.
What often blocks people is not imperfection, but self-reliance or pride disguised as certainty. Realizing this can either go in one direction or the other.  One being an unhealthy amount of shame, which is a trap itself.  The other is it becoming humility—the exact condition through which grace operates.
The Christian life is not: “I become powerful.” It is “Christ works through someone willing enough to let Him.” That does not always look like dramatic miracles. Sometimes the greater work is: bringing one soul back from despair, leading someone to Christ, forgiving when your instincts say not to, speaking truth when afraid, and enduring suffering without collapsing into bitterness.
Now, there are spiritual gifts given to humans, but not given to the human ego.  Because many would corrupt them. Scripture itself warns about this constantly. Miracles alone do not equal holiness. Even Judas performed ministry alongside the apostles.  The gifts are not meant to glorify the vessel.  They are meant to reveal Christ.
One last thing, when I pray at times, there is a doubting voice, very subtle, that says “you are not good enough, or your nature is sinful.”  I want to bring this up because this is not God’s voice.  Conviction from God is specific and leads toward repentance and restoration. Self-condemnation is crushing and paralyzing. It does the opposite; it steers you away from the loving embrace of God. 
Christ already knew Peter would deny Him three times and still entrusted him with the Church.  Christ fully knew human weakness before choosing to dwell among us… and chose us anyway. Not because we were already perfected, but because through Him we are being transformed.
